- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{6}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$

$$

$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2t+1\end{bmatrix}
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{bmatrix},
$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{b}_{1},{b}_{2}$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\left(\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\right)+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2t+1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}+3{a}_{2} \\ {a}_{1}-{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1}+3{b}_{2} \\ {b}_{1}-{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2t+1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0t+{a}_{1} \\ 0t+{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}({a}_{1}+3{a}_{2})t+({b}_{1}+3{b}_{2}+1) \\ ({a}_{1}-{a}_{2}-2)t+({b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+1)\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}+3{a}_{2}=0 \\ {a}_{1}-{a}_{2}-2=0 \\ {b}_{1}+3{b}_{2}+1={a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+1={a}_{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$
{b}_{1}=-1,\,{b}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

$$

$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}12t \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{t}-2{e}^{t}\cdot 2{e}^{-2t}}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -2{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{t}}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -2{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix} \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =-\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}12t \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4t{e}^{2t} \\ 8t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}-4t{e}^{2t} \\ 8t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int -4t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 8t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be re-written as 

$$
{J}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4x & 2y \\ 3{x}^{2} & 3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}4x & 2y \\ 3{x}^{2} & 3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{\begin{bmatrix}2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2 \\ {x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\ \begin{bmatrix}4(1) & 2(1) \\ 3(1)^{2} & 3(1)^{2}\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-\begin{bmatrix}2(1)^{2}+(1)^{2}-2 \\ (1)^{3}+(1)^{3}-1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be re-written as

$$
{J}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}-3xy+{y}^{2}-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}-3xy+{y}^{2}-1) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{3}-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{3}-2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}-3y & 2y-3x \\ 2x & 3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{t}-{e}^{t}\cdot 3{e}^{-2t}}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-{e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =-\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-5t{e}^{2t} \\ 15t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}-5t{e}^{2t} \\ 15t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int -5t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 15t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=-5t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-5\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -5t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(-5t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (-5\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}t{e}^{2t}+\frac{5}{2}\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}t{e}^{2t}+\frac{5}{4}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{e}^{2t}(1-2t).\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 15t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t & =15t\cdot (-{e}^{-t})-\int -{e}^{-t}\cdot 15\,\text{d}t \\  & =-15t{e}^{-t}+\int 15{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-15t{e}^{-t}-15{e}^{-t} \\  & =-15{e}^{-t}(t+1).\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}
$$

$$
{y}_{i}=2{\sum }_{j=1}^{3}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-{b}_{i},

$$

we have 

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}={x}_{j}$ if $i=k$, and

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=0$ if $i\ne k.$

This means that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{3}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =4{y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =4{y}_{i}{x}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

The $(i,j)$th entry of ${∇}_{A}L$ is $4$ times the $i$th entry of $y$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $x$, so

$$
{∇}_{A}L=4y\cdot {x}^{T}.
$$

Finally, evaluating ${∇}_{A}L$ at $A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{A}L & =4y\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =4(Ax-b)\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =4\left(\begin{bmatrix}3 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =4\left(\begin{bmatrix}15 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}64 \\ -4 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}128 & 192 \\ -8 & -12 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$
